title: Router First Setup
body:
Router first setup is the short job done the day a router arrives, before any device depends on it. The job is: change the admin password from its factory value, set a strong Wi-Fi password, turn on the router's automatic updates if offered, and write the new passwords somewhere safe. A router left on factory settings is an open door that every device behind it depends on.

The router is the one device every other device trusts, so its setup is the home's foundation.

The working method is router first-setup checklist. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Change the router admin password from its factory value at once
  2. Set a strong, unique Wi-Fi password
  3. Turn on automatic updates for the router if the option exists
  4. Turn off remote admin access unless it is genuinely needed
  5. Write the new passwords down and store them away from the router

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Admin password changed from factory value; OK :: Strong unique Wi-Fi password set; OK :: Automatic updates turned on; OK :: Remote admin access off; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Router interfaces differ, and some options have different names, so this record teaches the checklist rather than naming menu paths. Where a router offers no update option, its age and replacement plan matter more, which a later record covers. A common mistake is leaving the factory admin password in place because the Wi-Fi already works. title: Home Wi-Fi Passwords and Guest Network
body:
Home Wi-Fi passwords and a guest network divide the home's network into a trusted part and a visitor part. The main network holds family devices, while guests, visitors' phones, and untrusted gadgets join the guest network, which cannot reach the main network's devices. A strong main password and a separate guest password mean a visitor's compromised phone cannot wander into the family's cameras and computers.

Guests are welcome in a home without being welcome on every device in it, and networks should reflect that.

The working method is Wi-Fi password and guest-network setup. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Set a strong password for the main network and share it only with household members
  2. Turn on the guest network with its own password for visitors
  3. Check that the guest network cannot reach main-network devices
  4. Change the guest password after a large gathering or a stay
  5. Turn the guest network off when no guests are expected for a long stretch

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Main password strong and household-only; OK :: Guest network on with its own password; OK :: Guest network cannot reach main devices; OK :: Guest password changed after gatherings; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Not every router offers a guest network, and on older routers the separation may be partial. Where no guest option exists, the fallback is a second, cheap access point for visitors, or simply changing the main password after guests leave. A common mistake is handing out the main Wi-Fi password to every visitor, which quietly adds their devices to the trusted network. title: Smart Speaker and Camera Privacy
body:
Smart speaker and camera privacy is about the controls that decide when a device listens, watches, and keeps recordings. The controls to learn are: the mute or shutter switch, the recording history and its deletion, the voice and video retention setting, and which household members can review recordings. A device whose controls are unknown is a device whose recording habits are unknown too.

Speakers and cameras live in bedrooms and kitchens, so their privacy controls matter more than most settings.

The working method is speaker-and-camera privacy controls. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Find the physical mute or shutter control and test that it works
  2. Open the recording history and learn how to review and delete entries
  3. Set retention to the shortest period that still serves the household
  4. Decide who in the household may review recordings and agree it openly
  5. Place cameras where they never cover bedrooms, bathrooms, or guests' private spaces

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Mute or shutter control found and tested; OK :: Recording history reviewed; OK :: Retention set to the shortest useful period; OK :: Camera placement avoids private spaces; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Controls differ between devices and change with updates, so this record teaches the control pattern rather than promising a particular switch. It does not cover the law on recording others, which varies by place and needs local guidance. A common mistake is assuming a muted light means nothing is stored, without ever opening the recording history. title: Device Default Passwords
body:
Device default passwords are the factory credentials shipped with cameras, routers, printers, and many gadgets. They are printed in manuals and known widely, so any device still using one can be found and entered by anyone who knows where to look. Changing every default password at setup, and giving each device its own password where possible, closes the easiest entry point into a home network.

Factory passwords are public knowledge by design, which makes them the opposite of a secret.

The working method is changing factory credentials on every device. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List every connected device in the home on setup day
  2. Change each device's admin password from its factory value
  3. Give important devices, such as cameras, their own unique passwords
  4. Store device passwords in the household password store, not on notes stuck to devices
  5. Recheck defaults whenever a device is reset, since resets restore factory values

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: All devices listed on setup day; OK :: Factory admin passwords changed; OK :: Cameras given unique passwords; OK :: Passwords stored away from the devices; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Some devices offer only a single shared password or none at all, and this record does not pretend otherwise. Where a device cannot be given its own password, its place on the network matters more: put it on the guest network and limit what it can reach. A common mistake is changing the Wi-Fi password but leaving each device's own admin password at its factory value. title: Automatic Updates for Home Devices
body:
Automatic updates for home devices are the habit of letting devices patch themselves, and checking that they actually do. Updates fix known flaws, and a device that misses them stays open to anyone who reads the update notes. The routine is: turn on automatic updates where offered, check update status monthly, and replace a device whose maker has stopped offering updates.

An update note is also a public description of the flaw it fixes, which is why unpatched devices are found quickly.

The working method is keeping home devices updated. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Turn on automatic updates on every device that offers them
  2. Check each device's update status once a month
  3. Restart or allow a reboot when an update asks for one
  4. Note which devices no longer receive updates and plan their replacement
  5. Keep the router updated first, since every device depends on it

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Automatic updates on where offered; OK :: Update status checked this month; OK :: Pending reboots allowed; OK :: Router updated first; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Updates can occasionally change a feature or break a custom setup, which is why the routine includes a monthly check rather than blind trust. This record does not cover manual firmware installation, which needs the maker's own instructions. A common mistake is assuming updates happen because they were once turned on, without ever checking the status. title: Spotting a Stranger Device on Your Network
body:
Spotting a stranger device on a home network means reviewing the list of connected devices and recognizing each one. The router or an app can usually show device names, and the review asks of each name: do I know this device, and should it be here. An unknown device may be a guest's phone, a forgotten gadget, or an intruder, and the review is how the household tells the difference.

Most intrusions are discovered not by alarms but by someone noticing a name that should not be there.

The working method is reviewing connected devices for strangers. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Open the connected-device list on the router or its app
  2. Match each device name to a known household device or guest
  3. Rename known devices clearly so future reviews are easy
  4. Block or remove any device that nobody recognizes, then change the Wi-Fi password
  5. Repeat the review monthly and after any gathering

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Connected-device list opened; OK :: Every device matched to a known owner; OK :: Known devices renamed clearly; OK :: Unknown device blocked and password changed; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Device names can be changed by their owners, so a name alone never proves a device is safe, and a review cannot see devices that connect only briefly. The review is a habit that catches persistent strangers, not a guarantee of a clean network. A common mistake is ignoring an unknown device because the network still seems to work. title: Smart Lock and Doorbell Safety
body:
Smart lock and doorbell safety covers the devices that guard a home's entrances and record who approaches them. The practices are: give each person their own code rather than sharing one, remove codes when a person no longer needs access, keep a physical key as backup, and review doorbell recordings with the same care as camera recordings. A lock's convenience must never become a reason to skip the code hygiene a normal key would enforce.

A shared code is a copied key that cannot be taken back without changing the lock for everyone.

The working method is smart lock and doorbell practices. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Give each household member and helper their own entry code
  2. Remove codes promptly when access is no longer needed
  3. Keep a physical key as backup for power and network failures
  4. Review who can view doorbell recordings and set retention short
  5. Test the lock's behavior during a power cut and a network outage

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Individual codes issued per person; OK :: Stale codes removed promptly; OK :: Physical key kept as backup; OK :: Failure behavior tested; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Smart locks depend on power and network, and no record here promises they work in every failure mode. Households should test their own lock's failure behavior and keep a physical backup, and this record does not cover the law on recording visitors. A common mistake is sharing one code with everyone, including temporary helpers, and never changing it. title: Baby Monitors and Indoor Cameras
body:
Baby monitors and indoor cameras deserve the strictest home rules, because they watch the most vulnerable people in the most private rooms. The practices are: change default passwords, keep the camera's software updated, turn the camera off or cover it when not in use, limit viewing to named household members, and never place a camera where it can see a child undressed or asleep without a clear, agreed purpose.

A camera in a child's room is a window, and windows need curtains and locks, not just glass.

The working method is monitor and indoor camera practices. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Change the monitor's default password and give it a unique one
  2. Keep the monitor's software updated and check its status monthly
  3. Cover or switch off the camera when it is not actively needed
  4. Limit viewing to named household members and review the list
  5. Agree openly where cameras may and may not be placed in the home

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Default password changed; OK :: Software updated and checked; OK :: Camera covered when not in use; OK :: Viewing limited to named members; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. No camera is fully private once its images leave the home to a service, and this record cannot promise that any particular service keeps images secure. Households that need stronger assurance should prefer cameras that work locally without a remote service. A common mistake is leaving a monitor on its factory password because it was hard to set up the first time. title: Smart TV and Streaming Privacy
body:
Smart TV and streaming privacy covers what a television and its apps learn about viewing habits. Televisions can collect viewing data, voice commands, and app usage, and streaming apps can build profiles from watch history. The practices are: review the TV's privacy settings, turn off viewing-data collection where the choice exists, review each app's permissions, and sign out of apps on a shared TV when guests use it.

A television watches its viewers back, in data if not in pictures, and most households never open its privacy settings.

The working method is TV and streaming privacy settings. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Open the TV's privacy settings and read each data-collection choice
  2. Turn off viewing-data collection where the option exists
  3. Review permissions for each installed streaming app
  4. Sign out of personal apps before guests use the TV
  5. Repeat the review after major TV software updates

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: TV privacy settings reviewed; OK :: Viewing-data collection off where offered; OK :: App permissions reviewed; OK :: Personal apps signed out before guests; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Settings differ widely between TV makers and change with updates, so this record teaches the review pattern. It does not cover the content of any TV maker's privacy notice, which should be read for the specific model in use. A common mistake is assuming a TV is private because it has no camera, while ignoring its viewing-data collection. title: Voice Assistant Data Controls
body:
Voice assistant data controls are the settings that decide what happens to voice recordings and transcripts. The controls to learn are: how to review the history, how to delete individual recordings and the whole history, how long recordings are kept, and which household members can review them. A household that never opens its voice history does not know what its assistant has kept.

Voice recordings capture background conversation as well as commands, which is why their retention deserves a decision.

The working method is voice assistant history and retention. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Open the voice history and review what has been kept
  2. Delete recordings that are no longer needed, individually or in bulk
  3. Set retention to the shortest period that serves the household
  4. Decide openly who may review the household's voice history
  5. Use the mute control in rooms where private conversation happens

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Voice history reviewed; OK :: Unneeded recordings deleted; OK :: Retention set short; OK :: Review access agreed openly; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Use and limits. Deletion controls differ between assistants, and deleted recordings may persist in backups for a time, which this record notes honestly. It does not cover the law on recording others, which varies by place. A common mistake is assuming voice data is deleted because a command was answered, without checking retention. title: Home Network Segmentation
body:
Home network segmentation means splitting the home network into groups so that one compromised device cannot reach everything. The common split is three groups: trusted computers and phones, connected home devices, and guests. Cameras and gadgets live in their own group, which can reach the internet but not the family's computers, so a compromised camera cannot wander into private files.

Segmentation is the network version of locking interior doors: it limits how far an intruder can walk once inside.

The working method is separating device groups on the network. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List devices and sort them into trusted, home-device, and guest groups
  2. Place home devices on their own network segment where the router allows
  3. Check that the home-device segment cannot reach trusted computers
  4. Place guests on the guest network, never on the trusted segment
  5. Review the grouping whenever a new device joins the home

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Devices sorted into three groups; OK :: Home devices on their own segment; OK :: Home segment cannot reach trusted computers; OK :: Guests on the guest network; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Not every home router supports segmentation, and on simpler routers the guest network is the only split available. This record teaches the grouping principle so households can apply whatever split their equipment allows, and it does not promise any particular router feature. A common mistake is putting every device on one network because segmentation sounds complicated, and then discovering one weak gadget exposed everything. title: Firmware Checks and End-of-Life Devices
body:
Firmware checks and end-of-life planning answer the question every connected device eventually raises: is this device still supported. Firmware is the device's own software, and a maker that stops issuing firmware leaves known flaws unfixable. The routine is: check firmware status twice a year, note the maker's support statement, and plan replacement for any device that no longer receives fixes, rather than keeping it on the trusted network.

Devices do not announce their own expiry, and an unsupported device looks exactly like a supported one until it is attacked.

The working method is firmware status and end-of-life planning. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Check firmware version and update status for each device twice a year
  2. Find the maker's support statement for each device type
  3. Move unsupported devices to the guest network or disconnect them
  4. Plan and budget replacement for devices past support
  5. Record support end dates alongside the household device list

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Firmware status checked twice a year; OK :: Support statements found; OK :: Unsupported devices moved off trusted network; OK :: Replacement planned for past-support devices; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Support statements are sometimes vague, and a device may receive updates long after its official window or stop early. This record teaches the check and the move-to-guest-network fallback, not a promise about any maker's schedule. A common mistake is keeping an unsupported camera on the trusted network because it still works perfectly. title: Securing a Home Office Network
body:
Securing a home office network means giving work its own space on the home network, so work data and home gadgets do not share the same ground. The practices are: a separate network segment or at least a separate Wi-Fi name for work, a work device that family and guests do not use, and a rule that work material never travels to personal devices. The separation protects the worker's employer and the household equally.

Work from home blends two worlds on one wire, and the blend is where both worlds' risks meet.

The working method is home office network separation. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Create a separate segment or Wi-Fi name for work where possible
  2. Keep a work device that family and guests do not use
  3. Never move work material to personal devices or accounts
  4. Follow the employer's device and network rules where they exist
  5. Review the work segment whenever the home network changes

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Work segment or Wi-Fi name created; OK :: Work device reserved for work only; OK :: No work material on personal devices; OK :: Employer rules followed; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record does not override any employer's policy, and where an employer provides a managed device, its rules govern. It teaches the household side of separation, not corporate network design. A common mistake is letting family members use the work laptop for homework or games, which merges the two worlds completely. title: When You Sell or Give Away a Device
body:
When a device is sold or given away, its next owner must not inherit the previous owner's accounts, photos, passwords, or network access. The handover routine is: sign out of every account, remove the device from the account's trusted list, perform a factory reset, and, where the device stores data on a removable card, remove or wipe the card. A reset done before signing out can leave the device locked to the old account, so order matters.

A second-hand device is a second-hand diary unless it is wiped in the right order.

The working method is wiping and transferring a device safely. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Sign out of every account on the device before resetting
  2. Remove the device from each account's trusted-device list
  3. Perform a factory reset and verify the setup screen appears
  4. Remove or wipe any removable storage card
  5. Change the Wi-Fi password if the device knew it and the new owner is a stranger

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: All accounts signed out before reset; OK :: Device removed from trusted lists; OK :: Factory reset verified by setup screen; OK :: Removable storage wiped or removed; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Some devices retain data in ways a factory reset does not fully clear, especially older storage, and this record does not promise complete erasure for any particular device. For devices holding highly sensitive data, physical destruction of storage is the stronger answer. A common mistake is resetting without signing out first, which can leave the device tied to the old account. title: Whole-Home Safety Audit
body:
A whole-home safety audit is a once-a-year walk through every device, password, and setting in the home, done in one sitting with a checklist. The audit covers the router, Wi-Fi passwords, device passwords, update status, connected-device list, camera placement, and the household device list. Done annually, it catches the slow drift: the guest password shared too widely, the camera added and forgotten, the update that stopped arriving.

Home safety decays by drift, not by disaster, and only a scheduled audit notices drift.

The working method is annual whole-home safety audit. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Walk the router checklist: admin password, updates, remote access
  2. Review Wi-Fi and device passwords and the guest network
  3. Check update status and support for every device
  4. Review the connected-device list and camera placement
  5. Update the household device list and set next year's audit date

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Router checklist walked; OK :: Passwords and guest network reviewed; OK :: Update and support status checked; OK :: Connected devices and cameras reviewed; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. An audit is a snapshot, and a device added the week after it escapes notice until the next one. The record therefore pairs the annual audit with the monthly connected-device review, and it does not promise that any audit finds every problem. A common mistake is auditing only the router and calling the home done, while cameras and gadgets drift unexamined. title: Connected Devices for Renters and Shared Homes
body:
Connected devices for renters and shared homes face a special problem: the home's network and some of its devices may belong to a landlord or a housemate, not to the resident. The practices are: ask who controls the router and what is logged, use personal devices on a personal network segment where possible, agree openly which shared devices exist and who can view their recordings, and remove personal accounts from shared devices before moving out.

A shared home's devices are shared witnesses, and the sharing must be agreed, not discovered.

The working method is connected devices in rented and shared homes. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Ask who controls the router and what it records
  2. Agree openly which shared devices exist and who views their recordings
  3. Keep personal accounts off shared devices where possible
  4. Use a personal segment or hotspot for sensitive personal use
  5. Remove personal accounts from shared devices before moving out

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Router control and logging asked about; OK :: Shared devices and viewers agreed openly; OK :: Personal accounts kept off shared devices; OK :: Accounts removed before moving out; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record does not cover tenancy law or the legality of any recording, which varies by place and needs local guidance. It teaches the conversation and the hygiene that protect residents within whatever legal frame applies. A common mistake is assuming a landlord-provided device is private because it sits in your room.
